newsitem.title: GERMANY: Get away from it all for a fortnight - in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Get away from it all for a fortnight - in Albania.

text.p: Spare a thought for the man who has to sell Albania as a tourist attraction...
Fatmir Caci's stand, Albanian tours, was a small oasis of peace on Sunday as thousands of delegates fought for space at the world's biggest tourism fair in Berlin.
But although armed rebellion in Europe's poorest nation might have temporarily wiped out the tourist industry, it has failed to crush its representative's vision of things to come.
"There is not much interest in going to Albania at the moment," Caci conceded, "but we are looking to the future."
Albania, he said, has great tourist trap potential.
The brochures note the small Balkan country across the Adriatic from Italy has a sun-drenched climate featuring 2,400 hours of sunshine each year that puts it on a par with Greece.
But the tourism infrastructure, in a state of atrophy after 40 years of isolation under Stalinist rule, was only beginning to be built up before the eruption of violence last month.
"We have very little business here this year," said Caci.

Only about 10 people visited the Albanian Tours stand at the ITB, the travel industry's most important trade fair with more than 120,000 travel industry professionals and holiday planners attending the 177-nation exhibition.
Last year there were 150 business contacts that led to a number of tour groups to book trips to Albania.

"This year most of the people come here and ask me 'What on earth is going on in Albania at the moment?'" Caci said. "I try to explain that this could be the chance for a new start for us. This could clear away all the corruption."

Caci said that a bigger problem for Albania in the longer term was the lack of tourism infrastructure. Although the country has 300 km (180 miles) of Mediterranean coastline and several large lakes such as Lake Ohri, there are only 9,000 hotel beds in the country.
"That was the official policy of the communist government," Caci said. "They didn't want more than one hotel in each city because they wanted to keep close control of foreign visitors."

As a result, even before the outbreak of violence, Albania only had 80,000 foreign visitors per year. That is up from 20,000 per year during the communist era. But most of the visitors to Albania in recent years have been on business trips.
Caci said there were only 2,000 tourists in Albanian in all of last year.

"We are very optimistic about the future," he said. "We can understand no one wants to visit Albania right now. But if nothing else, all the media attention has helped for the longer term. It has informed the world about Albania."
